title: Squeeze locking pliers on a tube past their lock point with one gripper; whether they locked shows only on letting go
instruction: Clamp the locking pliers onto the metal tube at the orange band, level, so that they stay there on their own.
context: Welders and plumbers clamp locking pliers onto pipes and rods as a stop or a third hand. A spring holds the pliers open, so they stay on the tube only if the squeeze went past the lock point, where a latch at the handle ends catches. While the gripper still holds the handles shut, locked and unlocked pliers look almost the same (only the small orange latch at the handle ends moves a few millimetres); it shows when the robot lets go: locked pliers stay clamped, unlocked ones spring open and drop. The pliers are carried by the same two handles that close them, and because a parallel gripper closes both fingers toward its centre, the hand must slide sideways while squeezing so as not to drag the pliers off the tube. Unlike the vise and cam clamp tasks, where the clamp is fixed to the bench and closed by a screw or lever, or circlip pliers, which spread a ring and are not left in place, here a hand-held tool must be closed past its lock point on the part and left hanging there.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Tube: an aluminium tube, 2 cm across and 16 cm tall, fixed upright at x 36, y -12, with a 2 cm wide orange band of tape from 9 to 11 cm above the table. Pliers: steel locking pliers, 19 cm long, 160 g, preset for a 2 cm tube: jaws 4.4 cm long; two straight handles of uniform 9 by 14 mm rectangular cross-section with a thin red rubber covering, 124 mm fixed and 120 mm moving, with no enlarged central grip; the moving handle has a round steel latch pin at its end. They lie flat and open on two dark blocks (3 cm tall) with the pivot at x 25, y -24, jaws pointing forward (+x) and the moving handle on the left. Open, the jaws are 2.6 cm apart where the tube goes and the handles about 5.0 cm across at the grasp 3.5 cm behind the pivot; a spring holds them open (0.55 N m when open, 0.72 N m when shut). Squeezed shut, the handles are 3.6 cm across. At the end of the lower handle an orange latch on a spring (0.3 N per mm) slides along the handle; the upper handle's round end pushes it back over a 45 degree chamfer and it snaps over that end, holding the handles shut. The upper jaw has a sprung pad (8 N per mm); locked on the 2 cm tube it is pressed about 4 mm, a 32 N clamp.
scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a photo. 1.0 if the pliers are clamped on the tube by themselves (the tube between the jaws, the handles shut and held by the latch, the pliers 2 cm or more above the table and nothing touching them), with the jaws on the orange band (jaw centre 9 to 11 cm above the table), and level within 10 degrees (the trial ends early as a success once they have also been still, moving less than 1 mm, for 1 s); 0.5 if clamped by themselves but off the band or tilted more; 0.25 if the tube is between the jaws and the pliers are off the table but the robot is still holding them; else 0.
reset_notes: Push the orange latch back toward the handle end and let the handles spring open, slide the pliers off the tube and lay them open on the two blocks, pivot on the mark, jaws forward.
fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and cylinders; tube and holder blocks are fixed. The over-centre toggle of real locking pliers is replaced by a spring latch at the handle ends that snaps over the moving handle when the handles are squeezed shut; the jaws' give is a sprung pad (8 N per mm). The clamp force (32 N) is lower than real pliers so the robot gripper (about 50 N) can lock them. Jaw pad friction 1.2, other parts 1.0.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (1200 steps, seed 1); demo: 1.0 (498 steps).
